packages.title: The HOA fined me for a shed they approved in writing
packages.script: They fined me for THAT? The HOA mailed me a $500 violation for a storage shed it approved in writing 3 years ago. I had emailed the HOA board president before building it in my own backyard. She wrote back four words: approved, no issue. Last month, a brand-new board measured my yard against some outdated map and decided the approval had apparently evaporated. Very convenient expiration date. I forwarded her original email, timestamp and all, still sitting untouched in my inbox. The new board president went silent for 12 days. Then the fine dropped, a full year of dues was waived, and they rewrote the bylaw so a signed approval can never quietly vanish again. So who at the HOA is reading their own paperwork now?

shots.phrase: building it in my own backyard
measured my yard against some outdated map
forwarded her original email, timestamp and all
still sitting untouched in my inbox
a full year of dues was waived

packages.editor_note: Front-loaded the written approval and $500 reversal, tightened the deadpan escalation, and made the kicker explicitly name the HOA.

packages.title: Someone kept stealing my numbered parking spot at work
packages.script: My reserved spot, again? For 3 straight weeks, the same white SUV took spot 14—my assigned space, painted number and everything—every single morning. I left 2 polite notes on the windshield asking the driver to check the number. Nothing changed. Building policy says an unauthorized vehicle in a numbered spot after 2 written warnings gets towed at the owner's expense, no exceptions. Subtle system, really. On week 3, I called the property office, handed over my dated notes, and let them make the call. The SUV vanished from spot 14 around 10 a.m. The driver was 2 floors up, mid performance review, when someone texted him his car was gone. Tough meeting to sit through with THAT on your mind. So whose name is on spot 14 now?

shots.phrase: unauthorized vehicle in a numbered spot

Tough meeting to sit through with THAT on your mind
whose name is on spot 14 now

packages.editor_note: Front-loaded the repeated theft of spot 14, sharpened the tow payoff, and made the kicker explicitly return to spot 14.

authored_curiosity.title: Why Your Inflation Rate Isn’t the Official Number
authored_curiosity.hook: The government says prices rose 3.5 percent. Your grocery bill, rent, and gas tank may swear that number is fiction—but the number can be correct and still not describe you. The trick is hidden inside one enormous imaginary shopping basket, and almost nobody buys exactly what is in it.
authored_curiosity.closing: The official inflation rate measures the country’s basket. Your inflation rate is the receipt you actually carry home.
authored_curiosity.question: Which part of your budget feels furthest from 3.5 percent? Tell me below.
authored_curiosity.caption: The June 2026 Consumer Price Index rose 3.5 percent, but that does not mean every household’s costs rose 3.5 percent. CPI is a weighted national basket, while your real spending mix may lean harder toward shelter, food, gasoline, or medical care. Which part of your budget feels furthest from the headline number?

params.title: U.S. Consumer Price Index: All Items
params.source_name: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, Consumer Price Index — June 2026

segments.topic: what the official inflation rate measures
segments.say: Start with the headline. In June 2026, the Consumer Price Index for all urban consumers was 333.952, and prices were 3.5 percent higher than a year earlier. That number is real. But it is not a receipt from one average American. It is the movement of a giant weighted basket designed to represent spending across urban households. The index tells us what happened to that basket—not necessarily to yours.

params.title: CPI Basket Relative Importance
params.source_name: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, Consumer Price Index — June 2026

segments.say: The basket is weighted, and the weights do most of the magic. In the June table, shelter carried 35.149 percent of the index, food 13.447 percent, and energy 7.791 percent. Spend half your income on rent and almost nothing on gasoline, and your basket already looks different. Drive all day for work, own your home outright, or feed a large family, and it looks different again. CPI combines those lives into one national measuring stick.

params.title: U.S. Consumer Price Index: Shelter
params.source_name: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, Consumer Price Index — June 2026

segments.say: Shelter is the heavyweight. It was 35.149 percent of the basket and rose 3.3 percent over the year. Rent of primary residence rose 2.8 percent, while owners’ equivalent rent rose 3.3 percent. That last category estimates what homeowners would pay to rent their own homes; it is not a bill they receive. So two people can live under roofs that look identical while the index and their bank accounts tell very different stories.

params.title: U.S. Consumer Price Index: Food
params.source_name: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, Consumer Price Index — June 2026

segments.say: Food split into two different stories. Overall food prices were 3.0 percent higher than a year earlier. Food at home rose 2.7 percent, while food away from home rose 3.4 percent. Someone who cooks every meal did not buy the same inflation as someone who lives on restaurant food. Even inside the grocery aisle, the basket averages many categories together, so the item you buy every week can move much faster—or slower—than the food headline.

params.title: U.S. Consumer Price Index: Energy
params.source_name: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, Consumer Price Index — June 2026

segments.topic: why energy changes personal inflation quickly
segments.say: Energy is where the basket can snap sideways. Energy prices were up 15.7 percent over the year, and gasoline was up 26.7 percent. But gasoline also fell 9.7 percent in June alone. Both statements are true because one compares twelve months and the other compares one month. If you filled a tank that week, the monthly drop mattered. If you budgeted against last summer, the annual jump mattered. One product, two clocks, two completely different feelings.

params.title: U.S. CPI: All Items Less Food and Energy
params.source_name: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, Consumer Price Index — June 2026

segments.say: Economists often remove food and energy to see the slower signal underneath. In June, that core measure was up 2.6 percent over the year, below the 3.5 percent all-items rate. That does not mean food and fuel are unimportant; it means they are volatile enough to blur the underlying trend. Your household cannot remove dinner or commuting from its budget, which is exactly why a calmer economic indicator can feel nothing like daily life.

params.title: U.S. Consumer Price Index: Medical Care Services
params.source_name: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, Consumer Price Index — June 2026

segments.say: Now build your own answer. Hospital services rose 5.1 percent over the year, while used cars and trucks fell 1.8 percent. A household paying a hospital bill and buying no car experiences the first number, not the second. Another household may experience the reverse. The official 3.5 percent is not wrong; it answers a national question. Your personal inflation rate answers a different one: what happened to the exact things you bought, in the amounts you actually bought them?
